text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

Robusta futures in London, already at record highs, showed further sharp gains. Fund buying and a spill over arabicas sentiment drove July robustas to a high of $2,100 per tonne, up $45. September added $65 to close at $2,140 per tonne.

This week attention will focus on talks in London on Monday and Wednesday held by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to consider the future of its export quota program beyond June. The grouping could agree to defer plans to extend export quotas that were designed to keep a floor under world prices when they sagged last year.

Arabica futures in New York opened firmer but then corrected. The most important feature of note was the collapse of the May contract prior to expiration. The question is whether this is a warning signal that the situation has eased and that the end of the rally is in sight. However, that does not seem to be the case as fundamentals still point to tight supplies. July lost 6.90 cents/lb to close at 246.25 cents/lb while September gave up 6.35 cents/lb to close at 220.00 cents/lb.

Traders said today's downturn may have been aided by talk that the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) could lift export quotas in order to cool coffee futures. However, the question is, whether anybody adhered to the quotas anyhow given current high prices. At a preparatory session of the ACPC six-member technical group, a draft proposal for a full session on Wednesday would have the group retain export quotas but include new flexibility on allocating them, delegates said.

Also Brazilian coffee has gone to a steep discount, and that too might have undermined sentiment. However, some Brazilian sources still predict extremely low production figures for 1997/98 which, if realistic, should underpin prices.

BRAZIL - Brazil's government is still working with a 1997/98 coffee production forecast of 'about 20 million bags', Brazil's Minister for Commodities Mauricio Assis said. He added the estimate is down from production of about 25 million bags in 1996/97 because of climatic problems. He added the 20 million bag forecast was made earlier this year, and although the government continues to monitor crop progress, a more detailed estimate is not likely for some months.

Assis said 1997/98 exports are expected to total 15 million bags. Domestic consumption is pegged at 11 million bags, meaning that about 6 million bags will be withdrawn from stocks during the season. He said there are 12.9 million bags in stocks.

ICO - The ICO estimated 1996/97 (crop years) world coffee production at 96.5 million bags, up 12 per cent from 86.2 million in 1995/96. The 1996/97 figure is roughly 1 million bags below our own estimate. The ICO said production could be lower in 1997/98 if Brazilian output is as low as some are predicting.

CANADA - Canada imported 247,959 bags of coffee in January 1997, 28 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. Total imports in calendar year 1996 ros by 9 per cent to 2.739 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Guatemala (23,800 vs 24,100 bags), Brazil (36,400 vs 13,600 bags), Colombia (36,600 vs 50,000 bags) and Vietnam (22,600 vs 8,700 bags).

The country exported 33,900 bags of coffee in January 1997, sharply up from the 17,300 bags exported the same month the previous year. Total exports in calendar year 1996 rose by 18 per cent to 357,800 bags.

FINLAND - Finland imported 72,600 bags of coffee in January 1997, 43 per cent more than was imported the same month the previous year. Total imports in calendar year 1996 rose by 48 per cent to 1.120 million bags. Main suppliers of green coffee in January 1997 were Costa Rica (10,500 vs 2,200 bags), Brazil (18,900 vs 12,600 bags) and Colombia (17,400 vs 17,500 bags).

TURKEY - Turkey imported 207,500 bags of coffee in January/July 1996 which compares to 106,600 bags imported the same period in 1995. The main supplier of green coffee in January/July 1996 was Brazil with 173,200 bags, up from 83,400 bags shipped the same period in 1995.

AUSTRALIA - Australia imported 54,810 bags of coffee in March 1997, 21 per cent less than was imported the same month the previous year. That brought total imports since the beginning of 1997 up to 215,900 bags, 1 per cent less than was imported the same period in 1996. Main suppliers of green coffee in January/March 1997 were Vietnam (68,600 vs 77,800 bags) and Papua New Guinea (55,900 vs 58,700 bags).
